exchangesToWinRuling: docs/03-liars-assay.md How it plays: "First to five exchanges wins the duel."
offerRuling: errata 73 C: a boast whose counter Thad has not learned offers its three wrong answers; a learned one adds the right counter as a fourth, in a slot that varies by pair.
bystanderRuling: errata 73 F: a voice from the ring of chairs, unnamed.

pairs.boast: I pulled a nugget out of the Feather River the size of a bishop's fist.
pairs.counter: I've seen your bishop. He was malnourished.

wrong.text: That is a very large fist.
wrong.reply: It is. That's the point of the account.

wrong.text: I don't believe in bishops.
wrong.reply: Nobody's asking you to worship it, son, only to be impressed.

wrong.text: I have a small nugget.
wrong.reply: Then say so louder. That's how it's done.

pairs.boast: My claim assayed at nine hundred dollars to the ton.
pairs.counter: So did my grandmother, and she was mostly gravel.

wrong.text: Assayed by whom?
wrong.reply: By a man I trust entirely. I see him every morning when I shave.

wrong.text: That is forty-five cents a pound. I have done the arithmetic.
wrong.reply: Rule five, son. No arithmetic. It's on the wall.

wrong.text: Congratulations.
wrong.reply: Don't congratulate a man in an Assay. It looks like losing, because it is.

pairs.boast: I've washed more gold than you've washed shirts.
pairs.counter: That's true of everyone here, and it's a matter of some concern.

wrong.text: I send my shirts out.
wrong.reply: Then I've washed more gold than your laundress, and she won't mind hearing it.

wrong.text: I have four shirts. I am wearing the good one.
wrong.reply: That's an inventory, Grubb. Nobody bets on an inventory.

wrong.text: Gold does not need washing. It is famously inert.
wrong.reply: So's the audience, son. Look at them.

pairs.boast: My luck is famous from here to Sacramento.
pairs.counter: It's famous in Sacramento. That's why you're here.

wrong.text: I have never been to Sacramento.
wrong.reply: Then you'll have to take my word for it, and you just have.

wrong.text: Luck is what a man calls the parts he did not arrange.
wrong.reply: And the pencil calls it a point. Mark it.

wrong.text: I once found a dollar in a hymnal.
wrong.reply: Keep it. You'll want it for the fee.

pairs.boast: My strike was so rich the assayer wept.
pairs.counter: He weeps at everything. It's why we stopped inviting him.

wrong.text: The assayer is a woman.
wrong.reply: Then she wept prettily, and I lent her my handkerchief. Do keep up.

wrong.text: I would keep tears away from an assay. Salt affects the reading.
wrong.reply: Everything affects the reading, Grubb. That's what I'm counting on.

wrong.text: Was he all right?
wrong.reply: He'll live. You, I'm less sure of.

pairs.boast: I've had three fortunes and lost two.
pairs.counter: Then you've had one fortune and told it twice.

wrong.text: Which one did you keep?
wrong.reply: The one I'm telling you. It's the only kind that lasts.

wrong.text: Then you have one left. Could you lend me four dollars?
wrong.reply: I could. I'd want a deed for it.

wrong.text: Two out of three is a poor rate of keeping.
wrong.reply: It's a fine rate of telling, and telling's what's scored.

pairs.boast: I turned down ten thousand dollars for my claim.
pairs.counter: I was there. He offered four, and you cried.

wrong.text: That was foolish of you.
wrong.reply: It was. That's what makes it a good account. Nobody brags about the sensible thing.

wrong.text: I bought a claim from you for four dollars and a watch.
wrong.reply: So you know I've been through hard times, Grubb. Thank you for raising it.

wrong.text: Who offered it?
wrong.reply: A gentleman. I didn't catch his name, on account of the weeping.

pairs.boast: I've never filed a claim that didn't pay.
pairs.counter: You've never filed a claim.

wrong.text: I have filed one claim, and I regret it in detail.
wrong.reply: Regret's not scored, Grubb. Only the size of the thing.

wrong.text: Never?
wrong.reply: Never is the strongest word in the territory, son. I use it sparingly and on purpose.

wrong.text: Some claims pay in experience.
wrong.reply: That's what we tell the Eastern men, Grubb. Don't repeat it back to me.

pairs.boast: Every man in this territory owes me money.
pairs.counter: Every man in this territory owes someone money. You have described the territory.

wrong.text: I do not owe you money.
wrong.reply: Not yet. The afternoon is young.

wrong.text: Would you like it in writing?
wrong.reply: Nothing here is ever wanted in writing, Mr. Grubb. That's what keeps it cheerful.

wrong.text: Then you must be very rich, on paper.
wrong.reply: Paper's where all the money in this territory lives. It's the climate.

pairs.boast: There's more gold in my tailings than in your whole claim.
pairs.counter: There's more gold in my boot, and I would like it back.

wrong.text: You sold me my whole claim.
wrong.reply: And I'd know, wouldn't I. That's why it's a strong account.

wrong.text: What are tailings?
wrong.reply: What's left over, Grubb. You'll be one shortly.

wrong.text: That is a low bar, and I will not pretend otherwise.
wrong.reply: Pretending otherwise is the whole sport, son. You've just declined to play.

pairs.boast: My vein runs forty feet wide.
pairs.counter: So does the road, and it's about as productive.

wrong.text: Have you measured it?
wrong.reply: Measuring's for men who expect to be checked.

wrong.text: That is wider than this room.
wrong.reply: Everything's wider than this room. That's why we come in here to say it.

wrong.text: I have a vein in my temple that does something similar when I am lied to.
wrong.reply: Then you'll want to sit down, son. It's going to be a long afternoon.

pairs.boast: I've dug through solid granite with my hands.
pairs.counter: I have shaken your hands. They disagree.

wrong.text: Why would you not use a pick?
wrong.reply: A pick's for men with nothing to prove.

wrong.text: I tune pianos. My hands are the only part of me anyone has ever relied on.
wrong.reply: Then keep them in your pockets, son. The judges can see them shaking.

wrong.text: Did it hurt?
wrong.reply: Only the granite.

pairs.boast: There's a mountain named for me.
pairs.counter: There's a hole named for you. I have fallen in it.

wrong.text: Which one?
wrong.reply: The big one. You can't miss it, which is more than I can say for your counters.

wrong.text: I once had a dog named for me. It was a misunderstanding.
wrong.reply: And did it come when you called it? Mine doesn't either.

wrong.text: Mountains are named by surveyors, as a rule, not for prospectors.
wrong.reply: This one was named by me, son, which saved the surveyor a trip.

pairs.boast: I hired forty men to work my claim.
pairs.counter: I've met them. They are still waiting to be paid and they have formed opinions.

wrong.text: Forty is a great many men for a small claim.
wrong.reply: They were small men, Grubb. I hired them by the yard.

wrong.text: Are you hiring?
wrong.reply: Not tuners. Gold doesn't go flat.

wrong.text: I work my claim alone, with a raccoon in an advisory capacity.
wrong.reply: Then you're over-staffed by one raccoon.

pairs.boast: The gold came up so fast it followed me home.
pairs.counter: Everything follows you home. That is not gold. That is the dog.

wrong.text: Gold has no legs.
wrong.reply: Mine did. I'm sorry yours never learned.

wrong.text: Where do you live?
wrong.reply: Ask the gold. It found the place.

wrong.text: Nothing has ever followed me anywhere, except a bill.
wrong.reply: Then the bill knows something the gold doesn't.

pairs.boast: I found a nugget shaped exactly like the President.
pairs.counter: So did four men this month. It is a popular shape.

wrong.text: Which President?
wrong.reply: The one that's in, son. I'm a patriot.

wrong.text: Did it say anything?
wrong.reply: It said what Presidents say. I've forgotten it already.

wrong.text: I have a turnip shaped like the Vice President.
wrong.reply: Nobody remembers the Vice President, Grubb. That's a turnip.

pairs.boast: My father died rich.
pairs.counter: Your father died owing me two dollars, and I have chosen to regard it as a legacy.

wrong.text: I am sorry for your loss.
wrong.reply: Don't be sorry in an Assay, son. It's a forfeit.

wrong.text: My father died in debt, and he was very proud of how much.
wrong.reply: That's a better account than mine, Grubb, and you've wasted it on a counter.

wrong.text: Of what?
wrong.reply: Richness. It runs in the family.

pairs.boast: The Improvement Company came to me on their knees.
pairs.counter: The Company comes to everyone on their knees. It is how they get under the door.

wrong.text: The Company has been very courteous to me.
wrong.reply: Then they've not finished with you yet.

wrong.text: Were they proposing?
wrong.reply: They were, and I said I'd think about it, and I'm still thinking. That's called leverage.

wrong.text: That is also how I tune the bottom octave.
wrong.reply: Nobody here has heard a bottom octave, son, and the Company would charge it rent.

pairs.boast: I panned a pound before breakfast.
pairs.counter: You have never seen breakfast.

wrong.text: What did you have for breakfast?
wrong.reply: Gold, Grubb. Weren't you listening?

wrong.text: A pound troy, or a pound avoirdupois?
wrong.reply: A pound Vessel. It's heavier than both.

wrong.text: I am not at my best before breakfast either.
wrong.reply: That's an admission, Grubb. We don't do those in here.

pairs.boast: I once bought a saloon with a single nugget.
pairs.counter: I have been in it. You overpaid.

wrong.text: This saloon?
wrong.reply: A better one. This one I won at cards, which is more respectable.

wrong.text: What did you buy with the change?
wrong.reply: The bartender. He's been very loyal.

wrong.text: I would not know what to do with a saloon.
wrong.reply: You'd stand behind the bar, son, and the town would hand you its money. Hardest part's the apron.

pairs.boast: I know where Mott's strike is.
pairs.counter: So does everybody. That's the town. Try again.

wrong.text: Where?
wrong.reply: If I told you, son, it'd be your account, and I'm using it.

wrong.text: So do I, approximately.
wrong.reply: Approximately's where everybody keeps it. It's crowded.

wrong.text: Then why are you here and not there?
wrong.reply: Because there's no audience out there, Grubb, and a strike's no good without one.

pairs.boast: I built this town.
pairs.counter: You sold this town a map to a place that isn't there, and then sold it shovels.

wrong.text: It is a very nice town.
wrong.reply: Thank you, Mr. Grubb. I'll have that put on a plaque.

wrong.text: Some of it is level.
wrong.reply: The important parts, Mr. Grubb. I see to the important parts.

wrong.text: With your own hands?
wrong.reply: With other people's, which is the modern way.

pairs.boast: I have never been wrong about a claim in my life.
pairs.counter: You have been right about exactly one, Colonel, and you have spent twelve years making sure nobody digs it.

wrong.text: I have been wrong about several. I find it restful.
wrong.reply: Then rest, Mr. Grubb. Some of us have a town to run.

wrong.text: Neither have I. I have only had the one.
wrong.reply: Then we're both perfect, and only one of us owns the town.

wrong.text: That must be very lonely.
wrong.reply: Not at all. Being right draws a crowd, Mr. Grubb. Look around you.

mockery: That's not a lie, that's a remark.
You'll want to add a number to that.
There's a man in Sacramento who does that one properly.
I'll allow it, but the judges won't, and they're the ones with the pencil.
Son, you've told the truth. In front of people.

opening.speaker: sowerby
opening.line: 1. A man may not be interrupted in his account.

opening.speaker: sowerby
opening.line: 2. A man's account may be doubted only by a better one.

opening.speaker: sowerby
opening.line: 3. Truth is admissible but has never been raised.

opening.speaker: sowerby
opening.line: 4. The judges' decision is final, and may be appealed to the same judges.

opening.speaker: sowerby
opening.line: 5. No firearms. No knives. No arithmetic.

duel_one.openingRuling: errata 75: before the first exchange, Sowerby reads the handbill's five rules aloud, all of them.
duel_one.sequenceRuling: errata 73 D: pairs 1, 2, 3 and 4, then pair 1 again; nobody mutters on the repeat.
duel_one.notebookRuling: errata 73 D and 75: Thad writes each counter down as he hears it, and the notebook joins his repertoire when the duel is over.

loss.speaker: deke_vessel
loss.line: You've no account in you at all, have you.

loss.speaker: thad
loss.line: I have an account. It is scrupulously accurate.

opening.line: Then he will enjoy them twice.

duel_two.openingRuling: doc 03 Duel Two (errata 75): Sowerby, Vessel, Sowerby, and then "(He reads all five.)".
duel_two.orderRuling: errata 73 E, doc 57 B6 and errata 76 A: Tier 1 first, never repeating. Then, holding fourteen or more, the pairs Thad knows before the rest; holding fewer, the rest first (doc 02 B6: ">=14 pairs").

win.speaker: deke_vessel
win.line: Fine. Fine! I'll sign the cursed affidavit.

win.speaker: deke_vessel
win.line: You didn't enjoy that at all, did you.

duel_two.lossRuling: errata 73 H: a lost Duel Two ends on the reply that lost it; nothing more is said.
